4th Period.workingNow: Formatting the favorites list you already wrote, using your new HTML Quick Reference.
4th Period.weeklyDeliverable: A complete About Me page (copied from the Example file) with header/body structure, formatted favorites text, at least one image with a caption, and a table.
4th Period.smartGoal: I can apply bold, italic, underline, and heading tags to my existing favorites list so that it's easy to read, not just plain text.
4th Period.contentStandard: CA CS Standards 6-8.AP.13 — Create prototypes using structured code, organized into separate linked pages, to fulfill a design requirement.
4th Period.eldStandard: ELD.PI.6-8.6 — Reading closely and explaining orally how an author uses language to support ideas.
agenda: Hand out HTML Quick Reference sheet (3 min)
I do: model formatting one favorites item with <b> and <i> (8 min)
You do: format your own favorites list using at least 3 tags (15 min)
Exit Ticket: paste one formatted favorites line from your page (4 min)
4th Period.connections: Yesterday you got your favorites list written out and pushed. Today, since it's a short day, we keep it simple: format that same list using the tags on your new reference sheet — bold labels, maybe italics or underline for emphasis. Tomorrow we start on images.

6th Period.workingNow: Learning what pair coding is, then implementing your own state machine design with a partner in Sprite Lab.
6th Period.weeklyDeliverable: A Sprite Lab or Game Lab project where a scene or sprite has at least two states triggered by an event.
6th Period.smartGoal: I can pilot and navigate with a partner so that we implement our own state machine design in Sprite Lab.
6th Period.contentStandard: CA CS Standards 6-8.AP.12 — Design and iteratively develop programs that combine control structures, including compound conditionals.
6th Period.eldStandard: ELD.PI.6-8.1 — Exchanging information and ideas with others through collaborative discussions.
agenda: Hand back Monday's state machine design documents (2 min)
Mini-lesson: what is pair coding — pilot vs. navigator, and why we do it (6 min)
Get into pairs — whoever has the longer name pilots first today (2 min)
Pair coding Round 1: implement your design (9 min)
Swap roles — Pair coding Round 2 (9 min)
Exit Ticket: what's one thing your navigator caught or suggested? (2 min)
6th Period.connections: On Monday you sketched your own state machine design on paper — that's what's getting handed back today. On Tuesday you followed my example video step by step to build the tutorial's sprite. Today's different — you get your own design back and try to build it yourselves, with a partner. We're using pair coding: one of you pilots (drives the keyboard) while the other navigates (watches, catches mistakes, and calls out next steps), then you swap halfway through. Programmers pair up like this all the time — it catches bugs faster and forces you to explain your thinking out loud.
